summary:
What did you develop?
Journey to the Moon and Mars is a free 3D game that runs in the browser, for children aged 7–12, in English and Hebrew. It was built by 9th-grade students at ORT Aviation and Space School in Kiryat Gat, Israel. Players survive on the Moon, build a rocket, choose a destination, and run a Mars base for three sols, collecting real Perseverance-style samples.

How does it address the challenge?
Players balance oxygen, energy, food and radiation, and every choice has a cost. Each night they split limited energy between making oxygen (MOXIE), growing food, shielding and charging the rover. Real solar storms recorded by NASA trigger in-game radiation storms. Real measurements from Curiosity, Chang’e 4 and MOXIE keep the science accurate. Read-aloud cards, mouse-only play and changing storms make it easy to replay.

Why is it important?
Real missions depend on hard choices with limited resources. Our game turns space science from facts to memorize into decisions children make to survive. It shows them how NASA uses real data to keep astronauts safe.
details: Journey to the Moon and Mars is a free 3D browser game for children aged 7–12, in English and Hebrew. Players live through one full space mission: they crash on the Moon and survive by managing suit oxygen, energy and radiation, find six rocket parts and build the rocket like a puzzle, choose to fly to Mars, fly home to Earth or stay on the Moon, fly through real launch stages, and on Mars run a base for three sols, collecting six samples like the ones the Perseverance rover has gathered. Choices have a cost: running uses 1.5× the oxygen, solar panels work only in sunlight, and each Martian night players split limited energy between making oxygen (MOXIE), growing food in the greenhouse, radiation shielding and charging the rover. Real solar storms recorded by NASA (the DONKI database and NASA mission reports) decide when a radiation storm hits, and players must reach shelter in time. Children learn real physics and space science, such as gravity, radiation, thin atmosphere and solar power, by making decisions instead of memorizing facts. The game runs in any browser with no download or sign-up, can be played with a mouse only, offers read-aloud explanation cards for young readers, and stops the oxygen clock while they read; teachers can jump to the main stages with F + G + T. We want children to understand that space exploration depends on smart choices with limited resources and that NASA data keeps astronauts safe, and we hope to spark early curiosity about science and space careers, starting with a classroom pilot at our school. We wrote the game in HTML, CSS and JavaScript as a single file, using three.js for 3D graphics, the Web Speech API for reading aloud, Playwright with Chrome for automated testing, FFmpeg for the trailer, GitHub Pages for hosting, and Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant for coding, testing and preparing the trailer and presentation. Our data comes from NASA DONKI, NASA mission reports, and published measurements by Curiosity RAD, Chang'e 4, MOXIE and Perseverance. No special hardware is needed: we built it on regular laptops, and it runs on any computer with a modern browser. The game is creative because real space-weather data changes the gameplay itself, the challenge grows with the story from protecting yourself on the Moon to running a whole base on Mars, children see real consequences such as their radiation dose compared with NASA's career limit, and every game is different, with a new launch site, a different real storm season and three possible routes. Our team considered age fit (short sentences, icons, no reading under time pressure), scientific accuracy (real numbers come with their source, and game-only values like energy units and the shortened sol are marked as estimates), balance (we tuned the storm warning with a simulation so about 60% of players who run the right way reach shelter), accessibility (Hebrew right-to-left support, mouse-only play and read-aloud explanation cards), and privacy (no accounts and no personal data).
